entries.title: After Damen Silos demolition, city warns owner about code violations
entries.summary: <p>The owner of the site of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/18/damen-silos-demolition-starts-chicago-michael-tadin-jr-historic" >now-demolished Damen Silos</a> has been warned by the city for allegedly operating an “unauthorized” parking lot that was built without submitting a stormwater management plan.</p><p>City inspectors went to the site at 1910 W. 29th St. on June 18 and found that land was paved and was operating as a parking lot. The owner of the property had not submitted a plan to control stormwater runoff, according to the city.</p><p>The absence of a plan violated the city’s stormwater ordinance, the city said. Stormwater management is important for flooding control and also for protecting nearby waterways, such as the Chicago River. The lot also violated other zoning ordinances, according to the warning letter.</p><p>Michael Tadin Jr. and his family <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/12/27/23528364/damen-silos-sold-community-objections-preservationists-environmentalists" >acquired the Damen Silos</a> and the more than 20 acres of land where they once stood in 2022 from Gov. JB Pritzker’s administration for $6.5 million. Last year, the former grain silos, which had long sat dormant, were torn down.</p><p>The massive structures near South Damen Avenue along the Sanitary and Ship Canal were owned by the state for more than 90 years. They were a well-known landmark on the Southwest Side and were featured in the movie “Transformers: Age of Extinction.” A petition to save them was signed by more than 1,000 people.</p><p>In a statement Tadin said he doesn't believe he needs a permit because his parking lot does not create stormwater runoff. He also said it isn't permanent.</p><p>"This is a temporary pervious surface," the statement said, noting that it was being used by a neighboring business in a planned manufacturing area.</p><p>Tadin hasn’t said what he will do with the property. </p><p>“The owners have been advised to submit a formal plan in order to bring the site into full compliance with the code through a lawful building permit,” City Hall said in a statement. “Ownership was also advised to stop using the parking lot until compliance is established.”</p><p>The letter says the matter is being referred to the city’s law department and failure to correct the violations could result in potential fines of thousands of dollars a day.</p><p>Separately, Tadin owns MAT Asphalt in McKinley Park, which is a major city contractor. The plant also has been a source of odor complaints and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/12/14/24002009/mat-asphalt-pays-million-dollar-odor-lawsuit-settlement-michael-tadin-mckinley-park" >a class-action lawsuit </a>that paid out $1.2 million to neighbors.</p>

entries.title: The Reinsdorfs welcome new investors into the Bulls and United Center
entries.summary: <p>One of the richest franchises in the NBA is bringing on one of the richest families in the state of Illinois.</p><p>It was announced on Friday that Lukas and Samantha Walton have acquired a minority interest in both the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> and the United Center, but it will not affect the controlling interest the Reinsdorfs have in the team.</p><p>The Sun-Times reported several years ago that while the future of the White Sox was fluid at the time, the plan from both Jerry and Michael Reinsdorf was always to keep the Bulls in the family.</p><p>This latest news changes nothing as far as that was concerned, especially since the transaction involved purchasing limited partner stakes from existing LPs.</p><p>It does attach a huge financial name to the organization, however, as Lukas Walton, 39, is the grandson of Walmart founder Sam Walton.</p><p>The Reinsdorf and Wirtz families will also continue to hold the controlling interest in the United Center and The 1901 Project.</p><p>“We are pleased to welcome Lukas and Samantha, who share our deep-seated belief in Chicago and our commitment to the institutions that make this city strong,” team president and CEO Michael Reinsdorf said in a statement. “Together with our partners at the United Center, the Wirtz family, we are fully aligned in our vision for the Bulls, the United Center campus, and the future of the West Side.”</p><p>Jerry Reinsdorf — along with an investor group — purchased the Bulls in 1985 for $16 million and has watched the franchise grow to a value of over $6.45 billion since. That ranks the Bulls No. 5 in the Association of the current franchises, behind Golden State ($10.8 billion), New York ($10.1 billion), the Lakers ($10 billion) and the Clippers ($6.9 billion).</p><p>Jerry Reinsdorf is no stranger to selling pieces of a sports team, making headlines last year by striking a long-term agreement with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/05/jerry-reinsdorf-justin-ishbia-reach-long-term-agreement-that-establishes-a-framework-for-transition" >minority investor Justin Ishbia</a> to eventually transfer controlling ownership of the White Sox.</p><p>Ishbia will have the option to buy controlling interest starting as early as 2029.</p><p>This latest deal is nothing like that.</p><p>This was more about a foot in the door for the Waltons to also invest in Chicago’s West Side.</p><p>“The Chicago Bulls are as iconic as the city itself, and this transaction reflects our dedication to the city’s future,” the Walton’s said in a statement. “We have long admired the vision the Reinsdorf and Wirtz families have set forth for The 1901 Project, and we look forward to the United Center’s continued positive impact on Chicago’s West Side.”</p><p>Blackhawks CEO Danny Wirtz also expressed his enthusiasm about the transaction, stating, “Our families have had the great pleasure of partnering in the development of the United Center over the last 30 years and we look forward to a bright future ahead.”</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: Alcalde de Chicago da primer paso para crear un departamento nuevo para disminuir la violencia armada
entries.summary: <p>El alcalde Brandon Johnson emitió una orden ejecutiva el jueves para iniciar el proceso potencialmente costoso de cumplir con su promesa de crear un departamento municipal independiente que se enfoque exclusivamente en reducir y prevenir la violencia armada.</p><p>Dos días después de adoptar un plan que los alcaldes de Chicago han estado resistiendo durante más de una década, Johnson le dio sustancia a su propuesta.</p><p>Estableció una <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/06/23/funcionarios-y-lideres-de-chicago-piden-la-creacion-de-un-departamento-de-reduccion-de-la-violencia-armada" target="_blank" >Oficina de Reducción de Violencia Armada</a> dentro de la alcaldía y marcó procedimientos para apoyar el establecimiento de un departamento municipal permanente que coordine y fortalezca los esfuerzos desiguales de la Municipalidad.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4b0000" name="module-4b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Durante demasiado tiempo en esta ciudad, no hemos estado a la altura del desafío que enfrentan nuestros residentes ni con el nivel de inversión o de urgencia necesaria para trascender el abandono sistemático y la separación que han dejado cicatrices duraderas entre nuestras comunidades”, dijo Johnson durante una ceremonia de firma en la oficina del alcalde.</p><p>“Durante décadas, la gente ha exigido más del gobierno de la Municipalidad y hoy, el gobierno de la ciudad responde a esas demandas”.</p><p>Emmanuel Andre, vicealcalde de seguridad comunitaria, se desempeñará como director ejecutivo de la nueva oficina con un conjunto de órdenes contundentes. Estas incluyen recolectar datos sobre la violencia armada y las iniciativas de reducción de la violencia; emitir informes mensuales de progreso; identificar comunidades que han soportado el peso de la violencia armada y designar esos vecindarios más afectados como “Zonas Prioritarias de Seguridad Comunitaria”.</p><p>Andre también fue encargado de coordinar “inversiones e intervenciones integrales basadas en el lugar, adaptadas a las necesidades únicas” de cada una de esas comunidades.</p><p>La orden ejecutiva de Johnson también establece un Concilio Asesor de Reducción de Violencia Armada de 17 miembros, compuesto por una mezcla de profesionales de la salud mental, líderes religiosos y comunitarios, representantes de organizaciones filantrópicas y de organizaciones de intervención en violencia comunitaria. Nueve de los 17 miembros deben provenir de “vecindarios desproporcionadamente afectados por la violencia armada”, establece la orden.</p><p>La decisión de crear un nuevo nivel de burocracia en el Ayuntamiento —con al menos siete empleados y posiblemente más— llega en un momento en que los desafíos financieros de Chicago nunca han sido mayores. La Municipalidad enfrenta una crisis de pensiones de $36 mil millones y un déficit de $1.3 mil millones.</p><p>Con las elecciones de alcalde y concejales a sólo ocho meses, el debate sobre el presupuesto de este año probablemente será aún más contencioso que en los últimos dos estancamientos políticos, cuando el Concejo Municipal empoderado rechazó el aumento del impuesto a la propiedad propuesto por Johnson de $300 millones, así como su propuesta de impuesto a las corporaciones.</p><p>El presidente del Comité de Seguridad Pública, Brian Hopkins (2.º), dijo que no cree que Chicago necesite o que pueda permitirse crear más burocracia para combatir la violencia armada.</p><p>“No sé de dónde vendrán los fondos", destacó Hopkins. "Mi miedo es que el alcalde quiera financiar esto reduciendo el presupuesto de la policía. Y eso es absolutamente lo equivocado”.</p><p>No se mencionó en el comunicado de prensa del alcalde cuánto costará el nuevo departamento municipal ni cómo planea la administración de Johnson financiarlo. Chicago ya ha gastado docenas de millones de dólares en programas sociales destinados a reducir la violencia armada, así como en intervenciones comunitarias que buscan mediar y mitigar disputas relacionadas con pandillas antes de que ocurran.</p><p>Eso se suma al presupuesto del Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD) de $2.1 mil millones.</p><p>Johnson reconoció que Chicago ya está gastando más de $150 millones en combatir la violencia armada. "Eso, admito, no es suficiente”, dijo.</p><p>El alcalde añadió que las víctimas de la violencia armada son “abrumadoramente jóvenes, negros, niños y hombres” de entre 10 y 24 años. Las niñas afroamericanas también están convirtiéndose cada vez más en objetivos.</p><p>“Si alguna vez hubo un momento para que nos enfoquemos exclusivamente en un grupo particular que es más propenso a experimentar la violencia que conlleva el trauma, este es ese momento”, dijo.</p><p>La reverenda Ciera Bates-Chamberlain, directora ejecutiva de Live Free Illinois, dijo que ha “luchado por este momento” desde que los homicidios superaron los 800 durante la administración de Rahm Emanuel.</p><p>“Chicago es la mejor ciudad del mundo. Pero en demasiados vecindarios, la sombra de la violencia armada ha perdurado durante generaciones. Es hora de que nuestra infraestructura refleje la urgencia de esta crisis”, dijo.</p><p>Durante los primeros tres años de su administración, Johnson se unió a los exalcaldes Rahm Emanuel y Lori Lightfoot en resistir la presión para crear un nuevo nivel de burocracia en el Ayuntamiento. Pero el alcalde aparentemente cambió de opinión después de el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/22/8-dead-dozens-hurt-including-13-shot-during-juneteenth-party-over-holiday-weekend-in-chicago" target="_blank" >fin de semana de Juneteenth</a> que, como él lo puso, “debería haber sido una celebración”, y que, en cambio, fue “interrumpido por actos desgarradores de violencia armada” que dejaron ocho muertos y 40 heridos.</p><p>El estallido de violencia veraniega interrumpió lo que se ha convertido en su principal mensaje para los votantes de Chicago: reducciones históricas en el crimen y la violencia que llevaron a que la tasa de homicidios cayera en 2025 a su punto más bajo en 60 años. Otras grandes ciudades han registrado reducciones similares desde los máximos históricos alcanzados durante la pandemia.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Blackhawks wisely offload Andre Burakovsky to Senators for draft pick
entries.summary: <p>In the extreme sellers' market that exists in the NHL this summer, even the worst assets still hold value.</p><p>That fact was acutely demonstrated by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks?_gl=1*1tit1rh*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTI0MTI5MjkxMi4xNzgyNTAyMjk1*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODI1MDIyOTUkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODI1MDIyOTUkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' ability to trade veteran forward Andre Burakovsky to the Senators on Friday — hours before the draft — and get a 2027 sixth-round pick back for him.</p><p>Burakovsky, whose age curve seems to be hitting hard at age 31, struggled to a comical degree during the second half of last season, recording only four points in 37 games from Jan. 9 on — even while remaining stapled to Connor Bedard's wing for the majority of that time. </p><p>The Hawks were outscored 32-13 during Burakovsky's five-on-five ice time during that span, and his confidence eventually fell so low that turnovers became more common than completed passes. It was one of the most disastrous half-seasons by a individual player in recent memory.</p><p>"Things have not been coming easy," Burakovsky <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/03/02/blackhawks-andre-burakovsky-jeff-blashill-trust-confidence-connor-bedard-line" target="_blank" >said in March</a>. "But I've experienced this before in my career, where maybe you start doubting yourself a little bit and confidence is going down and it becomes harder to play."</p><p>Burakovsky is vastly overpaid, too, with a $5.5 million salary-cap hit on his contract that has one year left. Because of that contract, the Hawks were able to acquire him for essentially nothing from the Kraken last summer. In that trade, the return was Joe Veleno, whom the Kraken promptly bought out.</p><p>Burakovsky then seemed like a logical <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/07/blackhawks-andre-burakovsky-buyout-andrew-mangiapane-teuvo-teravainen" target="_blank" >buyout candidate</a> himself entering this summer. But thanks to this absurd trade market, he actually turned to be worth something. The Hawks didn't have to retain any salary, either.</p><p>The Hawks now own 11 picks in the 2027 draft, compared to just six in the 2026 draft (pending more moves Friday and Saturday).</p><p>Compared to what the Hawks gave up in their extremely bold trade for Bowen Byram earlier this week, this Burakovsky deal is a drop in the bucket, one that will have no effect whatsoever — unlike the Byram acquisition — on general manager Kyle Davidson's legacy. </p><p>But it's still remarkable in its own way.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Mientras la fiscal de los ‘Broadview Six’ enfrenta juicio, Boutros no escapa del peso que hay en su oficina
entries.summary: <p>La fiscal federal cuyas casi dos décadas de trabajo en Chicago están <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/22/broadview-six-damage-spreads-boutros-drops-more-charges-details-ongoing-review" target="_blank" >bajo la lupa</a> abordó una de las principales investigaciones de fraude de la Municipalidad antes de que el caso de los “Broadview Six” dio lugar a múltiples acusaciones de que había actuado de manera indebida.</p><p>Sin embargo, los abogados defensores que expusieron el presunto comportamiento irregular de la fiscal federal adjunta Sheri Mecklenburg dicen que la necesidad de rendir cuentas bajo la oficina del fiscal federal Andrew Boutros va más allá de una sola persona.</p><p>De hecho, la semana pasada pidieron a un juez que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/17/broadview-6-want-special-counsel-to-probe-boutros-office-trumps-justice-department-for-criminal-contempt" target="_blank" >nombrara a un fiscal especial</a> que investigara a Boutros y a otros por desacato penal, en parte “debido a lo que parece ser un esfuerzo decidido por culpar a un solo fiscal”.</p><p>Ahora, Boutros ha anunciado planes para revisar el trabajo de Mecklenburg desde 2007, un proceso que, según dijo, “probablemente llevaría a revisar las actas de más de 100 casos de gran jurado”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f40000" name="module-f40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Las acusaciones más significativas de Mecklenburg están dirigidas al exdirector financiero del Hospital Loretto, Anosh Ahmed. Pero también ha ayudado a asegurar penas de prisión para estafadores acusados de defraudar a grandes empresas privadas y a organizaciones benéficas.</p><p>No se ha anunciado ningún cambio en su situación laboral desde que estalló el escándalo el mes pasado. Un portavoz de Boutros refirió a los funcionarios del Departamento de Justicia en Washington, D.C., quienes no respondieron a un mensaje del Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Sergio Acosta, abogado de Mecklenburg, se negó a dar comentarios.</p><p>Boutros hizo su anuncio el lunes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >después de una serie de revelaciones</a> que llevaron a los jueces a preguntarse si todavía pueden confiar en la información proveniente de su oficina bajo una doctrina legal conocida como la “presunción de regularidad”. Se asume que los funcionarios federales actúan de buena fe.</p><p>Diez acusados en tres casos han visto sus cargos federales eliminados de manera permanente en el último mes, todos como resultado de la aparente mala conducta de Mecklenburg ante los grandes jurados.</p><p>Eso no incluye a tres acusados cuyos cargos fueron temporalmente retirados en medio de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/shooting-fbi-atf-hotaling-boutros-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >una controversia no relacionada</a> vinculada al intento de robo a agentes federales encubiertos en Country Club Hills.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e9bf0f" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Un collage de fotos de los llamados “Broadview Six”. Desde la parte superior izquierda: Michael Rabbitt, Brian Straw, Kat Abughazaleh, Andre Martin, Joselyn Walsh y Catherine “Cat” Sharp.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Siguen existiendo preguntas sobre el papel de Boutros y otros en el escándalo del gran jurado. Lo más importante, sigue sin quedar claro quién estuvo <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >involucrado en la redacción</a> de las declaraciones supuestamente inapropiadas de Mecklenburg incluidas en las transcripciones entregadas a la jueza de distrito April Perry en el caso de los “Broadview Six”.</p><p>Ese fue el caso de conspiración presentado contra seis manifestantes del Operativo Midway Blitz el otoño pasado.</p><p>Los fiscales entregaron a Perry las transcripciones redactadas en abril, dos meses después de que Mecklenburg abandonara la oficina del fiscal para un nombramiento temporal con el Comité Judicial del Senado. Los fiscales tampoco corrigieron a Perry cuando sugirió que las redacciones probablemente se debían a “problemas de computación”.</p><p>Cuando Perry finalmente tuvo en sus manos versiones no redactadas de las transcripciones, dijo que revelaban tres tipos de mala conducta procesal.</p><p>Mecklenburg presuntamente puso en juego su propia credibilidad para respaldar cargos penales, una práctica indebida conocida como “intercesión”. Exoneró a miembros del gran jurado que no estaban de acuerdo con el caso de los agentes federales, según muestran los registros. Y habló con ellos fuera de la sala del gran jurado, según las transcripciones. Pero Perry calificó las redacciones de “el asunto más problemático” de todos.</p><p>“Los errores suceden”, dijo Perry. “A todos nos pasa. Pero como les digo a mis hijos, asúmanlo. Admítanlo. Pidan disculpas y sigan adelante. Lo que no debe hacerse es ocultarlo”.</p><p>El fiscal federal adjunto William Hogan le dijo a la jueza, “Yo asumiré la responsabilidad por ello”.</p><p>Pero los abogados defensores insistieron más tarde en que “lo ocurrido durante el transcurso de esta acusación profundamente defectuosa claramente va más allá del error de cualquier fiscal adjunto de Estados Unidos”.</p><p>Se espera que la oficina de Boutros responda a la solicitud de un fiscal especial en el caso de los “Broadview Six” para el 7 de julio. Pero el lunes, Boutros reveló su plan para “garantizar la ausencia de irregularidades en el gran jurado” en los casos acusados y “restaurar la confianza del poder judicial, de la defensa y del público en las prácticas y procedimientos del gran jurado del distrito.”</p><p>La revisión de los casos de Mecklenburg formará parte de ese esfuerzo, destacó Boutros. Es probable que poco se pueda hacer respecto de los casos completamente resueltos, agregó.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Mecklenburg incluyen la acusación de fraude de 2017 contra un <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/5/15/18626863/corporate-credit-card-fraud-scott-kennedy-crystal-lundberg-nemera" target="_blank" >ejecutivo financiero de alto nivel</a> que le dio su tarjeta de crédito corporativa a una escort que había conocido en línea. Juntos, la pareja estafó a la empresa de dispositivos médicos Nemera por casi $5.8 millones.</p><p>Durante los argumentos de cierre en el juicio de 2019 de Crystal Lundberg, uno de los dos acusados, Mecklenburg le dijo al jurado que “no permitan que ella los engañe. Hagan que rinda cuentas. Hagan que asuma su responsabilidad”.</p><p>Lundberg terminó recibiendo una <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/12/9/21003599/former-escort-fraud-case-company-credit-card-prison" target="_blank" >sentencia de prisión de 53 meses</a>.</p><p>Mecklenburg también obtuvo una sentencia de prisión de 41 meses para un exdirector de una organización benéfica de niños discapacitados que supuestamente robó casi $1 millón de la organización.</p><p>No está claro si alguno de los dos casos formaría parte de la revisión del gran jurado de Boutros. Tampoco parece que Mecklenburg haya sido la fiscal que presentó la acusación formal en el caso de fraude de 2017. El director de la organización benéfica infantil se declaró culpable, renunciando a su derecho a una acusación formal.</p><p>Más recientemente, Mecklenburg participó en dos casos de fraude contra Ahmed y otros. Ocurrieron tras la controversia relacionada con la distribución de vacunas COVID-19 en el Hospital Loretto en Trump Tower, donde Ahmed tenía un condominio, lo cual fue reportado por primera vez por Block Club Chicago.</p><p>La oficina de Boutros <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >ya desestim</a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >ó los</a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" > cargos</a> contra acusados de “bajo nivel” atrapados en una de esas acusaciones después de que la jueza de distrito Sharon Johnson Coleman amenazara con llevar a cabo <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/10/hearing-in-loretto-hospital-case-could-address-claims-of-prosecutors-misconduct-if-feds-dont-drop-it" target="_blank" >una audiencia de evidencias</a> sobre la controversia del gran jurado en la oficina del fiscal.</p><p>Los fiscales evitaron esa audiencia al desestimar los cargos. Aun así, cuando los federales acudieron a la corte para hacerlo oficial, Coleman no se enfocó en Mecklenburg.</p><p>Más bien, la jueza preguntó, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/12/broadview-six-boutros-chicago-abughazaleh-justice-department-doj" target="_blank" >“¿Dónde está el Sr. Boutros?”</a>.</p><p>“No es un espectáculo en solitario”, dijo Coleman. “[Y] si hay un espectáculo de un solo hombre... es el fiscal de Estados Unidos. Él decide… Por eso tiene el trabajo importante”.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Sophie Sherry </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: 'Heat dome' forecast to bring dangerously high temps to Chicago area next week
entries.summary: <p>Dangerously hot weather could arrive this weekend as Chicagoans celebrate at Pride festivals, then persist throughout next week and into the July 4th holiday.</p><p>High temperatures are forecast in the 90s, with heat indices potentially surpassing 100 degrees, from Monday through Friday, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>Sunday, when Chicago’s 55th annual Pride Parade is scheduled, is forecast to reach 85 degrees, according to the weather service.</p><p>Whether the heat wave extends into July 4 depends on if storms that could cool the area develop next Friday, said NWS meteorologist Zachary Yack.</p><p>“If we don’t get the storms, then there’s a chance it could linger into next weekend. That’s the tricky and hard part to answer right now,” Yack said.</p><p>High air pressure entering the Midwest and eastern half of the U.S. is expected to “stay parked there” and create what’s referred to as a “heat dome” over the area, Yack said.</p><p>“When you have that, plus the summertime sunning, it all leads to just hot temperatures, humidity and, of course, those heat indices of more concerning and dangerous levels for those who are sensitive to heat,” Yack said.</p><p>Officials with the NWS and the Chicago Office of Emergency Management and Communications are urging residents to begin planning for the hot weather ahead of time.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">[3:25 PM CDT Friday 6/26/2026] The first bona fide heat wave of the summer is on the way next workweek. Take steps to prepare for the heat and plan ahead if you have outdoor activities scheduled! <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/ILwx?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#ILwx</a> <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/INwx?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#INwx</a> <a href="https://t.co/F2JGsJRBMp">pic.twitter.com/F2JGsJRBMp</a></p>— NWS Chicago (@NWSChicago) <a href="https://x.com/NWSChicago/status/2070604309658497058?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 26, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“If you’re going to be out and about next week, it’s best to make sure you have ways to stay hydrated, stay cool, so things like have water, cool drinks,” Yack said. “If you’re somebody who works outside, make sure you’re planning to wear lighter clothing. Prep that kind of stuff ahead of time.”</p><p>“During the heat wave, check on neighbors, friends, especially those who maybe have medical issues that the heat makes worse,” he said. “If you know a friend who doesn’t have air conditioning, reach out to them, make sure they’re doing OK.”</p><p>The city’s Department of Family and Support Services plans to open the following six cooling centers from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-70eeaa10-71b3-11f1-8664-2f7e5b466146"><li>Auburn Gresham Center, 1140 W. 79th St.  </li><li>Garfield Center, 10 S. Kedzie Ave. </li><li>King Center, 4314 S. Cottage Grove  </li><li>North Area Center, 845 W. Wilson Ave.  </li><li>South Chicago Center, 8650 S. Commercial Ave.  </li><li>Trina Davila Center, 4312 W. North Ave. </li></ul><p>Residents are also welcome to cool off at any of the Chicago Public Library locations, Chicago Park District fieldhouses, City Colleges of Chicago main campus locations and any of the Chicago Police Department’s 22 district stations, where people may also be connected to a shelter.</p><p>Well-being checks can be requested by calling 311 or visiting <a class="Link" href="http://311.chicago.gov" target="_blank" ><u>311.chicago.gov</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: Cubs hope changing scenery for David Peterson will get newly acquired lefty nearer to All-Star form
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — David Peterson was an All-Star last season.</p><p>But ever since his trip to the Midsummer Classic, it’s been a lot of poor results for the lefty pitcher, who the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> acquired in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/25/cubs-jed-hoyer-trade-mets-david-peterson-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-injuries-injured-list-bryse-wilson" >a Thursday trade with the Mets</a>.</p><p>After posting a 3.06 ERA before the break last year, he had a 6.34 ERA in the second half and has struggled to a 6.09 mark this season.</p><p>Saturday, for the first time in his decade-long pro career, he’ll be pitching for an organization other than the Mets, getting dropped into a battle for the NL Central as he makes his Cubs debut in Wisconsin.</p><p>It will be a new look for Peterson, with the Cubs hoping the change will do him good.</p><p>“There’s some aspect of this [being] a change of scenery,” Cubs skipper Craig Counsell said before Friday’s game. “We all can acknowledge that sometimes a change of scenery is a good thing.</p><p>“When things aren’t going well, sometimes a fresh start is something that can re-energize you, refocus you and hopefully get you to a good place. Hopefully, we can provide that.”</p><p>The big talking point in the wake of the deal — a long-gestating move that came to fruition once the Cubs gained urgency after righties Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown hit the injured list earlier this week — was that an infield stocked with Gold Glovers should greatly benefit Peterson, who has one of the higher ground-ball percentages in baseball.</p><p>Watching Mets infielders commit one error after another during the Cubs’ four-game sweep in Queens gave that argument some weight.</p><p>But even without digging into the specific differences between his new club and his old one, sometimes all it takes is a new logo to force a reset.</p><p>“When I was there, my whole goal and focus was to help the Mets win games. But I do think there is something to [the change-of-scenery thing],” Peterson said. “I’ve seen it with other guys, I’ve seen it with friends in the game, where they’re stuck in a rut or stuck in a spot that they’re not necessarily enjoying, and they go somewhere else and have a lot of success.</p><p>“That’s part of what gets me excited about this opportunity [along] with also joining a great team. … It’s definitely a thing.</p><p>“It wasn’t necessarily a thought of mine in New York of hoping for a change. I was committed to where I was at, just like I am now, committed to being here and helping these guys win.”</p><p>The Cubs need Peterson to deliver, not to justify parting with a former second-round draft pick in the trade but to stabilize a pitching staff ravaged by injuries.</p><p>If the Cubs are going to make it to a point where Jed Hoyer’s front office is seeking bigger upgrades to bolster a championship contender, they’ll need contributors like Peterson to help keep things afloat until the trade deadline gets closer.</p><p>That starts with results that are a lot better than what he produced in the last six months of baseball.</p><p>“You’re always trying to get better every day,” he said. “I went through some things early in the year that we needed to clean up and feel a lot better about where we’re at now, feel like myself back in ‘24, ‘25.</p><p>“It’s baseball. You’re going to go through waves. You’re trying to get better every single day and continue to hammer the good feels and mechanics and continue to do your homework and scouting on the guys you’re going to face.</p><p>“My goal is to be prepared every five days when I take the ball and give this team a chance to win.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Illinois AFL-CIO unlikely to withhold endorsements
entries.summary: <p>The news earlier this month that the Illinois AFL-CIO has “deferred” all decisions on legislative and statewide endorsements in the upcoming fall election generated quite a bit of headlines.</p><p>“Springfield not only failed to advance key priorities, but the process by which legislation was considered fell short of what working people deserve,” a statement by the state federation claimed. “These concerns span the full breadth of our movement, with public sector, private sector, manufacturing, and building trades all expressing dissatisfaction.”</p><p>The key priorities they pointed to included a multibillion dollar fix to the Tier Two pension system, which the state could not possibly fund without a significant tax increase. The unions also wanted <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?LegDocId=210482&DocName=10400HB2565ham002&DocNum=2565&DocTypeID=HB&LegID=160435&GAID=18&SessionID=114&SpecSess=&Session=" target="_blank" >House Bill 2565</a>, which would pay unemployment insurance benefits to striking workers after two weeks (expected costs are up to $1 million a year, but business interests were hotly opposed, and traditionally, no unemployment insurance changes can move forward without first being subjected to the agreed bill process — a tradition the AFL-CIO is trying to end). <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/BillStatus?DocTypeID=HB&DocNum=4416&GAID=18&SessionID=114&LegID=165070" target="_blank" >House Bill 4416</a> would grant unemployment insurance benefits to noninstructional education workers (cost estimated up to $176 million per year, and local schools were hotly opposed because they’d have to raise property taxes).</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-520000" name="module-520000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>And then there was the data center issue. Despite data centers being more unpopular than Ebola throughout the entire country (and the world, for that matter), enough House and Senate Democrats privately stood with organized labor against data center regulations deemed unreasonable by the industry that a bill which clamped down on them and would’ve been wildly popular never emerged. Heck, nobody ever got to the negotiation stage.</p><p>What upset some of the unions was that Gov. JB Pritzker decided to do what everybody has figured he’d do all along: He issued a decree pausing the granting of data center tax breaks until a legislative solution could be worked out.</p><p>That action will likely force the industry and the construction unions to the negotiating table. Even if a lawsuit is filed and won claiming that Pritzker overstepped his authority, the governor’s bureaucracy can still slow-walk applications — and everyone involved knows this.</p><p>To my eyes, this whole thing looks like member management. People don’t always realize that labor leaders are subject to similar election pressures as politicians. They have to keep their constituents happy, and in this case the constituency is the Illinois AFL-CIO’s executive committee. I just do not think that this announcement about how the union endorsement decisions will be “deferred” to a later date will wind up meaning no endorsements at all, for several reasons:</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-298285e1-719d-11f1-8eb3-5f06adbecd8e" start="1"><li>While things can change, this year is shaping up to be a horrible midterm for President Donald Trump in Illinois. The House and Senate Democrats are in no danger of losing seats (even Democratic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-house/2026/04/23/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-harry-benton-plainfield-lawmaker-democratic-caucus-ouster" target="_blank" >state Rep. Harry Benton</a>, who has been kicked out of the House Democratic Caucus over unspecified allegations, might actually pull this off, depending, of course, how horrible his oppo file is). The Dems might even win seats without spending a dime. Withholding endorsements only to see the Democrats go on to have a good year would be seriously counter-productive. The politics game is partially about making sure candidates believe they need you.<br></li><li><p> Organized labor has not been all that ecstatic about Pritzker. “He is labor friendly but not a friend to labor,” is a common refrain. So they’re hoping to use this threat of deferred endorsements to put a bit of fear into him as he gears up to run nationwide. But data centers are so absolutely unpopular with the electorate that Pritzker can point to his pro-labor record and explain that he just couldn’t be with his friends on this one. As far as pensions go, he can point to Illinois’ ignoble past of overpromising and underfunding pension benefits as a darned good reason to avoid repeating those mistakes. </p><p>When my associate Isabel Miller asked the governor about the announcement, Pritzker said the process was up to the AFL-CIO, adding that he considers himself "pro-worker." Neither of the two Democratic legislative leaders responded to requests for comment.<br></p></li><li> As noted above, several legislators stood with labor on data center regulation in private, and if unions did actually withhold their endorsements for the fall election, those folks would have no incentive to stick with unions in the future, at least on this topic.</li></ol><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-570000" name="module-570000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams vows to 'shut everybody up' by improving completion percentage in 2026
entries.summary: <p>Night games?</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams digs ’em.</p><p>That’s a good thing considering the NFL’s prime-time opinion of the upstart Bears, who are scheduled for “Monday Night Football” against the Eagles (Week 3) and the Seahawks (Week 8) in addition to a Thursday-nighter against the Patriots (Week 7), a Sunday-nighter against the Buccaneers (Week 9) and a Saturday-nighter against the Bills (Week 15).</p><p>“I love playing at night,” Williams said Friday on Barstool Sports’ “Pardon My Take” podcast. “It’s the game of the night. Nobody else is on. It’s us and the team on the other side of the ball, and let’s battle it out.”</p><p>As for playing in cold weather, also known as Bear weather?</p><p>Williams digs that, too.</p><p>“I love it,” he said. “I love playing in the cold. I actually love the cold more than any other weather, because my temperature [runs] hot. … I always feel that I play better when it’s cold and get better toward the end of the year.”</p><p>It’s almost as though this guy were made for fourth-and-everything in the waning moments of a January game under the lights at Soldier Field. The nearest Packer might even agree.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Caleb Williams made the throw of the year 4 different times 🎯 <a href="https://t.co/vYtpbqy1M1">pic.twitter.com/vYtpbqy1M1</a></p>— NFL (@NFL) <a href="https://x.com/NFL/status/2013401083683746088?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">January 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Williams would add a special ingredient in that scenario if he could: the chance to kick snow in the faces of critics who get bent out of shape because — a mere two seasons into his career — he completes a lower percentage of passes than most starters around the league and has a tendency to start slowly in games.</p><p>“Stats aren’t always something you should look at,” Williams said. “You should look at how they win games.”</p><p>Is he right? Be careful answering lest you get a sudden mouthful of slush.</p><p>“Obviously I want to get the completion percentage up, but some of the [good] things that I do on the field negatively impacts that,” he said. “But we’ll get it up anyway just to shut everybody up and help them understand. …</p><p>“We’ll get it up, we’ll make everybody’s heart feel warm and lovely, and it’ll also help us in the long run of winning games and starting games better, starting games faster, doing all those things.”</p><p>Headed toward a second training camp with coach Ben Johnson, Williams described their work together as “challenging.” Johnson is pushing him to be more decisive in attacking certain coverages, taking big shots when they’re there, being more trusting of his receivers to make plays and — still a major box to check — being better at hitting receivers in stride so they can pile up more yards after catches.</p><p>It’s called taking the next step toward superstardom. All the best QBs do it. Williams has a ways to go to get to the top tier even if EA Sports made him its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/03/bears-caleb-williams-madden-27-cover-revealed-quarterback-video-game-nfl-ea-sports" >Madden 27 cover man</a> — the first Bear to receive that honor.</p><p>Some of us who don’t play video games probably don’t quite get what a big deal that was.</p><p>“A childhood dream,” Williams said.</p><p>It seems there’s a dreaded “Madden curse” to worry about, except Williams isn’t worrying about it.</p><p>“We’re not going to mention it, but I don’t believe in those things,” he said. “I don’t think they’re real. We’re going to go prove it.”</p><p>If he’s right, it could mean more playoff wins are in store. It turns out Williams digs those, too. Who knew?</p><p>“It’s fun. It’s exciting,” he said. “And there’s a lot more coming.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/25/bears-qb-caleb-williams-application-to-trademark-iceman-nickname-denied-by-patent-office" >Bears QB Caleb Williams’ application to trademark Iceman nickname initially refused by patent office</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/25/nfl-power-rankings-how-do-the-bears-stack-up-against-the-leagues-heaviest-hitters" target="_blank" >NFL power rankings: How do the Bears stack up against the league’s heaviest hitters?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Last-place Mets fire manager Carlos Mendoza
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — From the front office to the field, just about everything has gone wrong for the New York Mets over the past year.</p><p>And on Friday, manager Carlos Mendoza took the fall.</p><p>Halfway through a wretched season, Mendoza was fired as skipper of the underperforming Mets and was replaced by Andy Green.</p><p>New York is 34-47 at the season's midpoint following a six-game losing streak (including getting swept by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> in a four-game series), 15 games behind NL East-leading Atlanta and 9½ games back of the NL's last wild-card berth.</p><p>Mets owner Steve Cohen had high expectations for a team without a World Series title since 1986. New York opened the season with baseball's highest payroll at $358 million and was projected to pay an additional $124 million in luxury tax.</p><p>"Our commitment to bringing our fans a championship-caliber team has not changed," Cohen said in a statement. "There is no sugar-coating it: This season has been a disappointment and our fans deserve better than what we've delivered."</p><p>At a Citi Field news conference ahead of Friday night's series opener against the rival Philadelphia Phillies, president of baseball operations David Stearns called it "a very difficult day."</p><p>"Mendy gave everything he had to our organization for the last 2½ years. He's an exceptionally talented leader. He's a really good baseball man. Above all else, he's an outstanding person. I enjoyed working with him and I'm going to miss him," Stearns said.</p><p>"Despite all of our effors, Mendy's included, we haven't been able to get this going this year. And I take responsibility for that."</p><p>Slowed by injuries to Francisco Lindor, Juan Soto, Clay Holmes, Luis Robert Jr. and Jorge Polanco, the Mets <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/25/cubs-jed-hoyer-trade-mets-david-peterson-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-injuries-injured-list-bryse-wilson" >traded pitcher David Peterson, </a>their longest-tenured player, to the Cubs on Thursday and could pivot to a selloff and retooling for the future.</p><p>Mendoza spent 15 seasons working for the Yankees, the last four as bench coach, before the Mets hired him to replace Buck Showalter after the 2023 season. New York advanced to the National League Championship Series in 2024 but failed to reach the playoffs last year and is among the sport's biggest disappointments this season.</p><p>Since starting last year 45-24 through June 12, 2025, the Mets are 72-102. That left the team with a 206-199 record under Mendoza, who was in the final guaranteed season of a three-year contract. He was hired by the Mets a month after Stearns joined New York as president of baseball operations.</p><p>"I understand there's no magic bullet here and there's no one change that immediately is going to turn this around," Stearns said. "This is incremental, this is day to day, this is doing the work every single day to get us back on track."</p><p>After signing Soto to a record $765 million, 15-year contract ahead of the 2025 season, Stearns made major roster changes last offseason. He allowed Pete Alonso to leave as a free agent and traded Brandon Nimmo, while bringing in Marcus Semien and Bo Bichette.</p><p>New York had a 12-game losing streak in April, its longest since 2002, and made six errors in the nightcap of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/24/cubs-dansby-swanson-grand-slam-two-homers-seven-rbis-pete-crow-armstrong-craig-counsell-offense-mets-doubleheader" >Wednesday’s doubleheader loss to the Cubs, </a>the team's most in a game since 2014.</p><p>"Carlos has led the organization with passion and grace and is beloved by everyone who works with him on a daily basis," Stearns said in a statement. "Carlos' impact on our players, staff, and culture over the last three seasons has been transformative. Unfortunately, we know we are falling short and change is necessary to move forward."</p><p>Green, a former major league infielder, joined the Mets in 2023 as senior vice president of baseball development and had been charged with running the farm system. He was given the title of interim manager for the rest of the season. Green managed San Diego to a 274-366 record from 2016-19, finishing with losing records in all four seasons.</p><p>Stearns said Green will return to a front-office role after this season and the Mets will conduct a full search for a new manager.</p><p>Green played four games for the Mets in 2009, his final big league appearances as a player. He became the fourth manager since Cohen bought the team from the Wilpon and Katz families after the 2020 season, following Luis Rojas, Showalter and Mendoza.</p><p>Mendoza is the third major league manager to lose his job since the season started. Boston's Alex Cora was replaced by Chad Tracy and Philadelphia's Rob Thomson by Don Mattingly.<br></p>

entries.title: Sky take hands-on approach to revive Azurá Stevens’ three-point shot
entries.summary: <p>Coach<b> Tyler Marsh</b> reached back in his player-development bag after shootaround, working out with forward <b>Azurá Stevens.</b></p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> signed Stevens to an expensive three-year deal to help space the floor around young center <b>Kamilla Cardoso</b>. So far, that part hasn’t clicked. Stevens has made only six of her first 40 three-point attempts since returning from injury.</p><p>“I’ve been working on trying to get more reps and seeing the ball go through,” Stevens told the Sun-Times earlier this week. “Just remembering that I can shoot. It’s hard when you don’t have shots going in. It’s really frustrating.”</p><p>Marsh was a player-development specialist on <b>Becky Hammon’s</b> staff in Las Vegas before coming to Chicago. He tinkered with Aces guard <b>Jackie Young’s</b> three-point shot, helping to fuel her breakout from beyond the arc.</p><p>After the Sky’s win against the Fire, Marsh noticed a few small things with Stevens, including her footwork, that he wanted to address.</p><p>“We don’t want her confidence to waver,” Marsh said. “I think she’s been turning down some open ones, and she’s missed some open ones. But we don’t want that to discourage her.</p><p>“Obviously, in this world, being a head coach, it’s a little bit harder to find individual time to be on the floor, especially in season, so you try to pick and choose and find the moments for it.”</p><p>It isn’t just Marsh, either. General manager<b> Jeff Pagliocca</b>, formerly a skills trainer, served up passes to Stevens after shootaround in Connecticut. The two have been discussing different things for her to focus on when she gets open.</p><p>Stevens has been improving in other areas. After a slow start on the glass, she is averaging eight rebounds over the last five games. She also is developing a nice high-low connection with Cardoso and averaging 3.2 assists in that span.</p><p>But the shooting remains the key. Stevens isn’t alone in her struggles. After a brief hot stretch spearheaded by <b>Skylar Diggins</b> and <b>Sydney Taylor</b>, the Sky have fallen back to a league-worst 23.6% from three-point range over their last three games.</p><h3><b>Not-free throws</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Shooting troubles have followed the Sky to the free-throw line.</p><p>Backup center <b>Elizabeth Williams</b> is shooting 37% from the line, worst in the league among qualifying players. Her form has a hitch: She rises onto her tiptoes, pauses, then releases while coming back down.</p><p>Williams told the Sun-Times on Wednesday that she is trying to adjust her process this season. She removed the dribble from her routine to create more fluidity.</p><p>“I’ve had different coaches try to modify [my free throws], but I think now it’s just getting it right,” Williams said. “Once I get it right, then the numbers will reflect that.”</p><p>As a team, the Sky shoot only 75% from the line, which has cost them games. But unlike some of their other problems, this one should be fixable.</p><h3><b>Go big or go home</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Sky will close their homestand against the Aces on Sunday afternoon at the United Center, their first of two games there this season.</p><p>The move is part of a larger WNBA trend: Teams that usually play in small or mid-sized arenas are moving select games into larger buildings. The Sky sold out both games at the United Center last season.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Chicago rapper Twista pleads guilty to not paying income taxes for 5 years
entries.summary: <p>Chicago rapper Twista has pleaded guilty to willfully failing to pay federal income taxes for five years.</p><p>The Grammy-nominated rapper, whose real name is Carl Mitchell, 52, did not pay income taxes amounting to roughly $175,000 between 2019 and 2023, according to a plea agreement filed in federal court last week.</p><p>A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Oct. 22. He faces up to one year in prison on each of the five counts to which he pleaded guilty.</p><p>Mitchell, who lives in south suburban Crete, has unpaid tax liabilities dating back to 2011. In all, he owes more than $440,000 in taxes, according to the Internal Revenue Service.</p><p>His lawyer could not be reached for comment.</p><p>From 2019 through 2023, Mitchell earned income from concerts, album sales, streaming and other royalties, the IRS said. He was informed several times by the IRS and his accountants of the taxes he owed.</p><p>But during those years, Mitchell also spent $100,000 for a Corvette, about $80,000 on a BMW I8, $65,000 for a Tesla and another roughly $65,000 on a Jeep, federal prosecutors said.</p><p>Mitchell “routinely made other large, non-essential purchases when he could have used available funds to pay his outstanding tax debts,” prosecutors said.</p><p>Mitchell also made an arrangement with a third-party company to pay him advancements for future royalties to avoid being taxed on them, according to the IRS.</p><p>According to the plea agreement, Mitchell will pay about $440,000 in restitution to the U.S. Treasury Department, as well as any interest and penalties.</p><p>Twista received two Grammy nominations in 2005 — one for best melodic rap performance on his song, “Slow Jamz” with Kanye West and Jamie Foxx, and the other for rap solo performance on his song, “Overnight Celebrity.”</p>

entries.title: Takeaways from Texas: Pritzker building state party coalitions that may prove helpful in 2028
entries.summary: <p>After helping Texas Democrats take refuge in Illinois amid a redistricting battle last year, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/06/26/jb-pritzker-donald-trump-texas-democratic-convention-speech" >came to Texas</a> on Friday to rally Democrats as they fight for their first blue statewide seat in 32 years. </p><p>The Democratic governor is also building coalitions in key states that could prove helpful should he run for president in 2028. </p><h3>Pritzker vs. Abbott</h3><p>Pritzker and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott have been publicly at odds since 2022, when Abbott started sending hundreds of thousands of migrants to Chicago.</p><p>Pritzker mentioned Abbott in his speech to the Texas Democratic Convention, saying he had been optimistic about his post-pandemic work as Illinois governor until the buses began to appear. </p><p>“My renewed optimism seemed warranted. Then Gov. Abbott bused 540,000 immigrants to Chicago, many in the middle of winter with no coats, left to brave the freezing temperatures with no food for their families,” Pritzker said. “And Abbott was unwilling to coordinate.”</p><p>Pritzker said the crisis represented President Donald Trump’s foothold on “the consciousness" of the nation: "Something dark and ugly flooded into our politics, as if a gate around our worst instincts had crumbled.”</p><h3>Pritzker is making inroads with state parties </h3><p>Pritzker is no stranger to fiery political speeches, including an April 2025 New Hampshire Democratic Party address that fueled 2028 presidential bid speculation. In that address, Pritzker blasted the Democratic Party for a “culture of timidity,” and said Republicans “cannot know a moment of peace,” words he later had to defend after Republicans like White House chief of staff Stephen Miller said were inciting violence. Pritzker pushed back and said he was referring to Democratic resistance, not violence.</p><p>State party addresses have given the governor introductions and also an opportunity to gain alliances in states he would need support from should he run for president in 2028.</p><h3>Democrats fighting back in red Texas</h3><p>Texas is trying to win a statewide Democratic seat for the first time since 1994 — and Pritzker has frequently been a cheerleader, in words and dollars, in battleground states. The Democratic governor on June 24 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/06/23/gov-pritzker-top-chicago-fundraiser-senate-candidate-james-talarico-texas" target="_blank" >hosted a fundraiser for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Chicago</a> — and he contributed $3,500 to his primary campaign in March. The race is expected to be one of the most expensive contests in the country. Talarico, a state representative, was among <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/08/18/texas-democrats-illinois-two-week-walkout-gop-remap-greg-abbott" target="_blank" >40 Texas House Democrats </a>who came to Illinois last year to deny Republicans a quorum needed to approve new maps to expand the GOP’s congressional majority.</p><h3>Pritzker is showing up in presidential polls, even slightly</h3><p>The Illinois governor has repeatedly laughed off questions about his political future and said he's focused exclusively on winning his third term for governor, but pollsters are indeed including Pritzker in presidential polls. Recent polls have shown Pritzker polling between 1% and 7%. An Emerson College poll conducted May 24 and 25 had Pritzker at 4%. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg topped that poll at 18%, followed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom at 16% and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 11%, according to a poll results <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/president-democratic-primary-polls-2028.html" target="_blank" >being collected by The New York Times</a>. A national poll conducted by Echelon Insights in April had former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel as an asterisk at less than 1%, Axios reported. </p><h3>Pritzker leaning in on Democratic Party critiques, not just Trump-bashing</h3><p>Pritzker spent much of his speech talking about the need for the Democratic Party to account for its mistakes and to rebuild. Prior to the 2024 presidential election, Pritzker placed most of his focus on critiquing Trump. </p><p>In his Friday speech, Pritzker blamed Democratic Party leaders for growing “complacent” and “letting nostalgia for parts of our political past replace efforts to innovate our political future.”</p><p>“Unwilling to break old customs to build new foundations, it seems like everyone on our side thought democracy was a garden that didn’t need tending, forgetting that weeds need to be pulled up by their roots, not just occasionally mowed down,” Pritzker said.</p><p>At a Chicago event on June 16, Pritzker said Democrats running for president need to focus "not just on restoration, but also a renewal of American values."</p><p>“I think <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/06/16/gov-pritzker-potential-2028-presidential-run-democrats-have-lost-our-way" target="_blank" >Democrats over the years have kind of lost our way.</a> It’s very important to me that we actually follow through," Pritzker said. </p>

entries.title: Chicago's Haitian and Syrian communities in limbo after Supreme Court decision: 'Playing with people's lives'
entries.summary: <p>For Ludovic Comeau and many other Haitian-Americans, this week has been loaded with emotional whiplash. He celebrated Haiti’s appearance in the World Cup Wednesday, only to learn Thursday that refugees from his country were denied temporary protected status by the nation’s highest court.</p><p>In a ruling Thursday, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to move forward with ending the 36-year-old temporary protected status program, ending legal status for hundreds of thousands of Haitian and Syrian migrants — and potentially millions of others from countries across the globe.</p><p>“We don't like what's happening," said Comeau, an economics professor at DePaul University. "[And] we still look for little moments of pride, being happy that we are Haitians. … We will never stop loving the United States because it was a good haven for us when we needed help.”</p><p>But for around 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians in the U.S. with temporary protected status, the U.S. may no longer be a “haven” at all. If they can’t find a legal way to stay in the country, they face deportation back to countries still plagued by violence and instability.</p><p>Additionally, the decision opens the door for migrants from other countries to be denied temporary protected status, raising questions about the future of American immigration policy.</p><p>“This also serves to dismantle broader guarantees for refugee status and 14th Amendment guarantees,” said Katy Arnold, who runs the Refugee and Forced Migration Program at DePaul University.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </figure> </div> </div><p>For Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, a son of Haitian immigrants, the decision is personal. </p><p>"In my hometown of Chicago, we recognize a Haitian man, Jean Baptiste Point DuSable, as our first settler who had the vision that the land we now know as Chicago could be a center of trade in the Midwest," Raoul said in a statement. "To allow for the termination of TPS status for Haitian Immigrants in this manner ignores the specific mandates of the TPS statute, current conditions in Haiti and the many contributions made by Haitians to this country.”</p><p>Ali Tarokh came to the U.S. as a refugee from Iran. Now, in his position as director of development and communications at the Syrian Community Network, he’s watching fellow refugees from neighboring Syria and Haiti face the very real prospect of uprooting their lives in the U.S.</p><p>“That [Supreme Court] decision is playing with people's lives," Tarokh said. "Over the years, they have become our neighbors, coworkers and friends. They have opened small businesses, worked in health care and education, raised their children in American schools and contributed to the communities that welcomed them."</p><div class="Enhancement" She said legal advocates are still unsure of the timeline when things like work permits will expire for those affected.</p><p>She suggested anyone looking for help to reach out to the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights or related groups like Access to Justice and the Resurrection Project.</p><p>Fred Tsao, senior policy counsel at ICIRR, recommended getting legal guidance entries.title: City officials, police emphasize safety ahead of Chicago Pride Parade
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police and city officials put a heavy emphasis on public safety Friday as they outlined plans for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lgbtq/2026/06/26/what-to-know-about-chicagos-2026-pride-parade-route-street-closures-and-more" >55th annual Chicago Pride Parade</a> stepping off on Sunday.</p><p>Officials said the Chicago Police Department, the Office of Emergency Management and Communications, and parade organizers worked for months to ensure the parade through Lake View and Lincoln Park stays a safe and welcoming environment.</p><p>"We are ready to secure the parade route and safeguard the community area before, during and after the parade," said CPD Chief Angel Novalez. "We will maintain a visible presence to ensure everyone is able to safely enjoy this parade that honors the strength and diversity of our LGBTQ+ community."</p><p>Officials acknowledged that over the years the largest safety concerns occur once the official parade ends, often leading to spontaneous gatherings that could lead to disorder or violence.</p><p>"We know that nighttime activity in the area following the parade can turn into disorderly and potentially violent situations," Novalez said. "Violence, vandalism or criminal activity will not be tolerated."</p><p>Novalez did not reveal any specific operation details, but he did share that CPD reviewed after-action reports from previous years to identify gaps in its response plans. The department has since added supervisory personnel to respond more quickly if multiple incidents occur.</p><p>Center on Halsted CEO Jolie Robinson said the emphasis on security this year comes as LGBTQ+ communities have faced heightened threats across the country.</p><p>"We know that there is a national climate of folks being targeted because they are a part of the LGBTQ+ community," Robinson said. “We've seen language directed toward our transgender community that is troubling and harmful, and so not only is this an important day of celebration … but also it's about how we ensure that everybody that's coming out in celebration of this beautiful day is and can be safe.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/22/federal-trade-commission-world-professional-association-transgender-health" >Federal Trade Commission sues Chicago-area transgender health group</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/16/school-districts-trans-kids-pay-anti-trans-lawsuits" >School districts, trans kids pay for anti-trans lawsuits cropping up across U.S.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><p></p><p>Ald. Bennett Lawson (44th) said the event remains an important symbol of inclusion at a time when LGBTQ+ communities continue to face challenges across the country.</p><p>"With continued attacks on the community all across the country, the Pride Parade sends a strong message that Chicago is a safe and welcoming space for everyone," he said.</p><p>Lawson said in addition to the police department's safety efforts, the parade route has been shortened and the number of entries has been reduced in order to aid public safety.</p><p>Ahead of temperatures rising this weekend, officials also encouraged attendees to drink water and cool off when necessary. The parade will also include cooling stations for attendees if needed, along with trucks to provide workers with water and snacks. The parade will begin at 11 a.m on Sunday and will conclude at 2 p.m.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami's autographed rookie card sells for $75,000
entries.summary: <p>Before losing him to a hamstring injury last month, signing Munetaka Murakami clearly paid off for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>.</p><p>Now, a 9-year-old from Arizona is also reaping the benefits.</p><p>Mason Deane, who collects trading cards, lucked into a box of Topps cards in April that contained a one-of-one redemption for a Murakami autographed rookie card, according to a story from <a class="Link" href="https://www.12news.com/article/news/local/valley/arizona-9-year-old-sells-rare-baseball-card-for-nearly-75000-after-lucky-pack-pull-chicago-white-sox-murakami/75-818bd7c2-9456-4766-ac4e-5279b5bde521" target="_blank" ><u>Arizona television station KPNX.</u></a></p><p>"It's something that's fun to do with your son. We have what we call a trading business, and we just buy and sell baseball cards," Mason’s father Bradley told KPNX.</p><p>"We normally just look around, and if I feel lucky, we get a pack," Mason added.</p><p>"I was like, 'This is crazy.' I'd never heard of a card like that," he said.</p><p>The family decided to put the card up for auction and sold it for $75,000.</p><p>"I was like, 'Oh, wow. That's a lot.' I was just surprised," Mason said.</p><p>Mason wanted to use the money to buy more cards. Bradley overrode his son’s wishes and put the cash in a college fund.</p><p>The family intends to travel to Chicago next month to meet Murakami and take in a Sox game at Rate Field.</p><p>"That's
